paras: The whipping of Black brakemen at Lufkin, Texas, was a mob attack in the summer of 1903 in which two Black brakemen of the Houston, East and West Texas Railroad were taken from a caboose and severely whipped, after which the mob fired into the car. No one was reported killed, and no arrests appear in the coverage. The episode drew notice outside Texas mainly because Lufkin's Commercial Club publicly condemned the mob and offered a reward, a response the New York Sun praised in an editorial that other papers reprinted.

The surviving accounts give no exact date, and the Sun, writing on August 18, placed the attack only "the other day." According to the Sun, a mob took the two "negro brakemen" from a caboose in Lufkin and whipped them "severely." The mob then returned to the car and fired several shots into it, narrowly missing the conductor, whose race is not given. The brakemen are not named, and no accusation against them or other cause for the attack is reported.

Members of the Lufkin Commercial Club and other citizens met, condemned the proceedings of the mob, and offered a reward for the arrest and conviction of "the rioters." Their resolution pledged "a prompt and speedy punishment of any further outrageous conduct toward the colored people of this town and county." By August 16 a Bryan, Texas, paper had noted that the club "has taken strong action against lawlessness" and offered rewards for "recent offenders." No report of an arrest, prosecution or payment of the reward was found.

Texas coverage found is a single line in the Bryan Morning Eagle, which described the club's action without mentioning the attack, its victims or their race. The fuller account comes from an editorial in the New York Sun headed "Good for Lufkin!", which mocked the mob as "Invigorated by the exercise" and called the resolution "especially commendable." The Sun's praise rested on economics as much as humanity: it called the resolution "sound business sense, as well as humane feeling" and argued that, "Southern labor being mainly negro labor," no Southern town could afford to have Black workers injured by mobs.

The editorial travelled through exchange columns, appearing in the Wilmington Evening Journal on August 21 and the Arizona Republican on August 27 under the same headline. The Richmond Times-Dispatch reprinted it on August 30 as "The Texas Way," placing it beneath comment from the Chicago Record-Herald on recent lynchings in Illinois. No Black-press coverage of the attack was found.

reader.title: Whipping of Black brakemen at Lufkin, Texas
bases: A mob seized and whipped two Black railroad brakemen and fired into their caboose (A2); no organized band, warning or stated motive is reported, so the attack is coded as a mob assault rather than whitecapping.

The attack itself is described only in the New York Sun editorial (A2) and its reprints (A3, A5, A6); the earlier, independent Bryan item (A1) confirms only that the Lufkin Commercial Club acted against 'recent offenders' and offered rewards.

accounts.gist: A mob took two Black brakemen from a caboose, whipped them, and fired into the car, after which the Commercial Club and citizens condemned the mob, offered a reward and pledged to punish further outrages against Black residents.

framing.detail: The Bryan Morning Eagle gave the Commercial Club's 'strong action against lawlessness' one line, without describing the attack or its victims.

The New York Sun headed its editorial 'Good for Lufkin!', mocked the mob as 'Invigorated by the exercise', and praised the resolutions on the ground that 'no Southern town can afford to have colored laborers interfered with'.

The Wilmington Evening Journal and Arizona Republican reprinted the Sun editorial under 'Good for Lufkin', and the Richmond Times-Dispatch ran it as 'The Texas Way.' beside comment on Illinois lynchings.
